body: Seconding what was said in the discussion, I think it's important to mention what exactly this does and the benefits, like "if a certain amount of capacity is reserved, subsequent `push_backs` will be faster until the size gets bigger than that".

body:
Thanks for the feedback :)
We've reached a conclusion in the last core meeting to _not_ expose this function to GDScript for now, as it's not that useful in comparison (and potentially confusing against `resize`). So my next push will remove this change anyway!
Is `[[nodiscard]` really needed? For most use cases, I think this just enforces unnecessary error handling.

A failed `reserve` allocation is almost certainly going to lead to undefined behavior afterwards (e.g. from failed `push_back` calls), so it would be good if callers need to consciously handle this.

Other, similar APIs such as `resize` currently don't force callers to handle this case, which I think is a mistake.  Of course, this is somewhat of a departure from our current API design, and it may turn out to be annoying for other developers. I still think it's the right call, but I'm open to discussing or changing this!

I also agree with @DeeJayLSP and wouldn't add the `[[nodiscard]]`.

Effectively if this happens, if this doesn't crash, something else will .. I think as an engine Godot has positively taken the decision to not handle out of memory conditions (in most cases), and so forcing call sites to add error handling code goes against this.
Allowing containers to have a signed size, the gift that keeps on giving... :grin:

Not that I'm suggesting it is wise to do much alloc failure handling, but is there any guarantee that a realloc to a smaller size can't fail?
Grok suggests it is less likely than a grow, but it is not guaranteed.

If it can shrink by e.g. decommiting pages or another method that is one thing, but if it has to create a smaller buffer then copy, it's still allocating more than was there originally?

Still I guess you'd _hope_ a sane implementation to detect it can't allocate second buffer, and just return without changing the size.

Hrm, yea I guess depending on the allocator implementation, a shrinking realloc may actually fail.
I'll adjust accordingly.

My only concern here is that the reserve function supports a wider range than the resize, for uniformity I'd suggest using `int` to not create strange cases, you could easily have cases where you do `reserve(size)` followed by operations adding elements or resizing triggering errors or weirdness as the size isn't supported
Good point. `int` is for sure a mistake but it's consistent with the rest of the class. I'll make it `int` for now and make a note to update the interface to use `int64_t` in the future.
